approaches.name: Safe zones for pins or screws in the humeral shaft
approaches.corridor: Anterolateral deltoid window in the proximal third (protecting the axillary nerve), no percutaneous corridor in the middle third, and a posterior or open-lateral window in the distal third that visualizes the radial nerve

sources.title: Safe Zones For Percutaneous Pins Or Screws
Safe zones for percutaneous pins or screws (humerus)

procedure_applications.condition: Temporary external-fixator pins are placed in the humeral shaft

positioning.text: Support the arm so proximal-lateral and, if the patient is not strictly supine, posterior distal pin sites can be imaged. In a supine polytrauma patient the posterior distal corridor is usually inaccessible.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the acromion (axillary nerve about 5–7 cm distal), the deltoid insertion, and the olecranon fossa. There is no percutaneous safe zone in the middle third.

incision.text: Use a formal incision large enough to palpate or see the nerve. Do not use stab incisions, especially if a distal pin must sit laterally near the radial nerve.

superficial_interval.text: Proximally go (antero)laterally through deltoid, avoiding the axillary nerve and long head of biceps. Distally the classic corridor is posterior through triceps; if a lateral pin is forced by positioning, open enough to see the radial nerve.

deep_interval.text: Advance pins so the tips just perforate the far cortex. Do not place pins in the middle third. Distally stay out of the olecranon fossa.

layers.text: Skin, deltoid or triceps, periosteum, then humeral cortex, with the axillary or radial nerve identified before drilling.

structures_at_risk.text: The axillary nerve and long biceps tendon proximally, the radial nerve on the middle and distal dorsal shaft, and the median nerve and brachial artery if a distal pin is driven too deep, are at risk.

danger_zones.text: The middle third has no percutaneous safe zone because the radial nerve hugs the dorsal cortex. Over-penetration medially threatens the neurovascular bundle. Distal over-penetration threatens the median nerve and brachial artery.

retraction_hazards.text: A posterior distal pin can irritate the triceps and make bed positioning uncomfortable; if a lateral pin is chosen instead, visualize the radial nerve rather than retracting blindly.

exposure.text: Each site is only a pin window. The distal-humerus page recommends a mini-open technique whenever humeral pins are required.

limitations.text: The posterior distal corridor is usually unavailable in a supine polytrauma patient. The middle third cannot be pinned percutaneously.

indications.text: Used when external-fixator or percutaneous pins must be placed in the humeral shaft through defined proximal or distal corridors.

closure.text: Close the mini-open windows after confirming the nerve is free of the pin.

complications.text: Complications include axillary-nerve injury, radial-nerve palsy from a middle-third or unseen lateral pin, and median-nerve or brachial-artery injury from an over-long distal pin.

questions.question: Is there a percutaneous safe zone in the middle third of the humerus?
questions.answer: No. The radial nerve is too close to the dorsal cortex.

questions.question: How far below the acromion does the axillary nerve typically run?
questions.answer: About 5–7 cm, dorsolaterally around the metaphysis.

questions.question: If a distal pin must be placed laterally in a supine patient, what is required?
questions.answer: An incision large enough to palpate or see the radial nerve; no stab incisions.

approaches.name: Dorsal approach to the fifth carpometacarpal joint
approaches.corridor: Curved dorsoulnar incision along the fifth metacarpal that turns radially over the hamate, retracting the little-finger extensors radially and the dorsal sensory ulnar nerve with ECU ulnarly

sources.title: Dorsal approach to the carpometacarpal joints

procedure_applications.condition: A fifth-metacarpal-base intra-articular fracture, 5th CMC fracture-dislocation, or ECU avulsion is exposed dorsoulnarly

positioning.text: Position the hand pronated so the dorsoulnar fifth ray and hamate are accessible.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the fifth metacarpal, the hamate, the ECU insertion on the ulnar fifth-metacarpal base, and the course of the dorsal sensory ulnar nerve.

incision.text: Make a curved cut along the dorsoulnar fifth metacarpal that turns radially over the hamate. The dorsal sensory ulnar branches are especially vulnerable in the proximal third.

superficial_interval.text: Protect the dorsal sensory ulnar nerve and longitudinal veins. Retract the little-finger extensors radially with their loose tissue, and retract the sensory nerve ulnarly, often with ECU.

deep_interval.text: Make a longitudinal capsulotomy for intra-articular fractures, or extend an existing capsular tear. If the joint is not opened, mark it with a needle or K-wire and check on the image intensifier before placing screws.

layers.text: Skin, dorsal sensory ulnar nerve and veins, little-finger extensors and ECU, dorsal capsule, then the fifth CMC and hamate.

structures_at_risk.text: The dorsal sensory branch of the ulnar nerve, longitudinal veins, little-finger extensors, and the ECU insertion are at risk.

danger_zones.text: The proximal third of the incision is the danger zone for the dorsal sensory ulnar nerve. Blind screws can enter the CMC joint.

retraction_hazards.text: Retract radial sensory branches radially and ulnar sensory branches ulnarly rather than stretching a nerve across the field.

exposure.text: Exposes the fifth CMC for base fractures, fracture-dislocations, and ECU avulsions.

limitations.text: This window is specific to the fifth ray; widely separated radial CMC injuries need a separate tendon-respecting incision.

indications.text: Indicated for intra-articular fifth-metacarpal-base fractures, 5th CMC fracture-dislocations, ECU avulsions, and rare displaced extra-articular fifth-metacarpal-base fractures.

closure.text: Cover implants with periosteum, repair any divided intertendinous connection, and close skin without trapping the sensory nerve.

complications.text: Complications include dorsal sensory ulnar neurapraxia or neuroma, extensor adhesion to uncovered metal, and intra-articular screw penetration.

questions.question: Where is the dorsal sensory ulnar nerve most vulnerable?
questions.answer: In the proximal third of the incision as it curves over the hamate.

questions.question: Where does ECU insert?
questions.answer: On the ulnar side of the fifth-metacarpal base.

questions.question: How can the joint be marked if a capsulotomy is not made?
questions.answer: With a hypodermic needle or small K-wire checked on the image intensifier.
